# Psalm 50 — Verse-by-Verse Commentary Notes

## Overview / Structure

The psalm is a dramatic courtroom scene: God Himself is Judge, summoning the whole earth as audience while He tries His own covenant people. The traditional structure (found in Spurgeon, Ellicott, Cambridge Bible, and others) is:

- **vv. 1–6:** Prologue — the Divine Judge appears in theophany and summons heaven and earth.
- **vv. 7–15:** First speech — rebuke of empty ritualism (duty toward God / the first table of the Decalogue).
- **vv. 16–21:** Second speech — rebuke of hypocritical wickedness (duty toward neighbor / the second table).
- **vv. 22–23:** Epilogue — warning to the forgetful, promise to the thankful and obedient.

— Ellicott (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/50.htm); Spurgeon, Treasury of David (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tod/psalms-50.html); Cambridge Bible (snippet in search results, https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/cambridge/psalms/50.htm); Enduring Word (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-50/)

---

## Verses 1–3: The Mighty One Comes to Judge

**v. 1: "The Mighty One, God the LORD, speaks and summons the earth from where the sun rises to where it sets."**

- The Hebrew stacks three divine names: *El* (Mighty One), *Elohim* (God, a plural of majesty/intensity), and *Yahweh* (LORD, the covenant name). This triple title appears only here and in Joshua 22:22. It is like a royal herald proclaiming a monarch's full titles before a decree. — Ellicott (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/50.htm); Gill (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/50.htm); Pulpit Commentary (search snippet: "A combination of three names of God…only found here and in Joshua 22:22"); Enduring Word (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-50/), citing Morgan, Maclaren, and VanGemeren.

- Gill notes that some (Jarchi, Kimchi) read "El, Elohim" as "God of gods" or "Judge of judges," and sees the three names accented distinctly with a singular verb as hinting at a mystery of the Trinity. — Gill (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/50.htm)

- "From the rising of the sun to its going down": the summons is universal — all mankind is called to hear. — Spurgeon (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tod/psalms-50.html)

- Gill interprets the whole psalm as referring to the Gospel dispensation — the calling of the Gentiles, the abrogation of legal sacrifices, and God's controversy with the Jews for rejecting spiritual worship. — Gill (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/50.htm)

**v. 2: "From Zion, perfect in beauty, God shines forth."**

- Zion is called "the perfection of beauty" because the Temple, the residence of Jehovah, was there. — Ellicott (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/50.htm); Pulpit Commentary (search snippet); cf. Psalm 48:2; Lamentations 2:15.

- "God shines forth": the Hebrew verb (*yaphia*) means to scatter rays from afar, a magnificent flashing light — used of God's glorious appearing. — Spurgeon (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tod/psalms-50.html), citing Venema.

- Spurgeon adds: God shines not only *in* Zion but *out of* her — the church's beauty is seen by all when God shines forth from her. Gill sees this as Christ shining forth in the Gospel from the church under the new dispensation. — Spurgeon (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tod/psalms-50.html); Gill (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/50.htm)

**v. 3: "Our God approaches and will not be silent! Consuming fire precedes Him, and a tempest rages around Him."**

- The imagery is borrowed from the giving of the Law at Sinai (Exodus 19:16–19), but this time God comes to Zion, not Sinai. — Enduring Word (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-50/), citing Kidner and Spurgeon.

- "Will not be silent": God had been silent in patience; now He comes to speak in judgment. Augustine is quoted: "He kept silence that he might be judged, he will not keep silence when he begins to judge." — Spurgeon (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tod/psalms-50.html); Enduring Word (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-50/)

- Fire and tempest are emblems of justice and overwhelming power. — Spurgeon (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tod/psalms-50.html); Constable (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/psalms-50.html)

- Gill applies fire and tempest to the destruction of Jerusalem and the temple. — Gill (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/50.htm)

## Verses 4–6: Judgment Begins with God's Own People

**v. 4: "He summons the heavens above, and the earth, that He may judge His people:"**

- Heaven and earth are called as witnesses or assessors in the divine courtroom (cf. Deuteronomy 4:26; 32:1; Isaiah 1:2; Micah 6:2). — Ellicott (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/50.htm); Pulpit Commentary (search snippet: "the inhabitants of heaven — the holy angels"); Constable (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/psalms-50.html)

- The shocking twist: God summons the whole earth, but then turns to judge *His own people* first, not the pagan nations. This is the principle Peter later articulated: "judgment begins at the house of God" (1 Peter 4:17). — Enduring Word (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-50/), citing Kidner; Spurgeon (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tod/psalms-50.html); Constable (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/psalms-50.html)

**v. 5: "Gather to Me My saints, who made a covenant with Me by sacrifice."**

- "My saints" (*chasidim*): Ellicott says this verse is of great importance as a formal definition — the "saints" are those in covenant with God, a covenant ratified by sacrifice. — Ellicott (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/50.htm)

- Pulpit Commentary argues that "My saints" here means *all Israel*, the whole nation — not just the godly, because the covenant by sacrifice encompassed the entire nation (Exodus 24:3–8). This is the visible people of God, not only the elect. — Pulpit Commentary (search snippet)

- Spurgeon takes a more discriminating view: the gathering is for separation — the false will be convicted and the true revealed. Those who have truly ratified the covenant by faith in the great propitiatory sacrifice (Christ) will be attested; mere formalists will be exposed. — Spurgeon (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tod/psalms-50.html)

- The phrase "made a covenant" (literally "cut a covenant") alludes to the ancient practice of slaying and dividing victims in solemn covenant rites. — Enduring Word (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-50/), citing Alexander.

**v. 6: "And the heavens proclaim His righteousness, for God Himself is Judge. Selah."**

- The heavens (the angelic host) declare that God's judgment is righteous. — Ellicott (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/50.htm); Pulpit Commentary (search snippet); Constable (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/psalms-50.html)

- Ellicott adds a fine touch: order and law in the physical world are evidence of an ordered moral government — the obedient stars challenge man to submit consciously to the same will. — Ellicott (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/50.htm)

- "Selah": a pause for meditation, perhaps a musical interlude. — Gill (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/50.htm)

---

## Verses 7–15: Rebuke of Empty Ritualism

**v. 7: "Hear, O My people, and I will speak, O Israel, and I will testify against you: I am God, your God."**

- God addresses Israel as His covenant people. The phrase "I am God, your God" echoes the opening of the Decalogue ("I am the LORD thy God") and reminds them of their unique privilege and responsibility. — Spurgeon (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tod/psalms-50.html); Enduring Word (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-50/)

- Gill sees this as an address to the Jews who were about to have "Lo-ammi" (not my people, Hosea 1:9) written upon them for refusing to hear the great Prophet. — Gill (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/50.htm)

**v. 8: "I do not rebuke you for your sacrifices, and your burnt offerings are ever before Me."**

- The point is *not* that they neglected sacrifice — they were scrupulous in it. The problem was that they thought sacrifice was all God required. They had the outward form but not the inward devotion. — Ellicott (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/50.htm); Constable (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/psalms-50.html); Enduring Word (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-50/)

- "Ever before Me" can be read as irony: their sacrifices are *continually* there — God has had enough of them. — Pulpit Commentary (search snippet)

**vv. 9–11: "I have no need for a bull from your stall… for every beast of the forest is Mine — the cattle on a thousand hills. I know every bird in the mountains…"**

- The argument is that God already owns everything. Pagan religions imagined that gods needed to be fed by sacrifices; Yahweh reminds Israel He has no such need. — Constable (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/psalms-50.html); Enduring Word (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-50/), citing Maclaren and Spurgeon.

- Ellicott calls this passage "a fine tone of irony." — Ellicott (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/50.htm). Ellicott also notes that the LXX and Vulgate read "hills of oxen" rather than "a thousand hills." — Ellicott (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/50.htm)

- There is a "note of sarcasm" in the pronouns: the people proudly say "my bull…my stall…my pen," and God answers with emphatic "Mine…Mine…Mine" (vv. 10–12). — Constable (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/psalms-50.html), citing VanGemeren.

- Enduring Word tells the story (perhaps apocryphal) of Harry Ironside praying when Dallas Seminary was near bankruptcy: "Lord, the cattle on a thousand hills are Thine — please sell some and send us the money." A rancher then arrived with a check from selling two carloads of cattle for exactly the needed amount. — Enduring Word (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-50/)

**v. 12: "If I were hungry, I would not tell you, for the world is Mine, and the fullness thereof."**

- God's self-sufficiency is absolute. He does not depend on human offerings. — Gill (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/50.htm); Constable (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/psalms-50.html)

**v. 13: "Do I eat the flesh of bulls, or drink the blood of goats?"**

- A rhetorical question exposing the pagan notion (common in surrounding cultures) that deity literally consumed sacrifices. — Gill (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/50.htm); Enduring Word (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-50/), citing Cresswell: "Pagan sacrifices were considered as feasts of the gods."

**v. 14: "Sacrifice a thank offering to God, and fulfill your vows to the Most High."**

- The "sacrifice" God really wants is thanksgiving and loyal performance of vows — not that outward rites should cease, but that the inward must animate the outward. — Ellicott (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/50.htm); Pulpit Commentary (search snippet: "The one offering acceptable to God is praise and thanksgiving out of a pure heart.")

- Gill notes the Jewish tradition that in the Messianic age all sacrifices will cease except the sacrifice of praise. — Gill (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/50.htm)

**v. 15: "Call upon Me in the day of trouble; I will deliver you, and you will honor Me."**

- God desires a living trust — prayer in trouble, not mere ritual performance. This verse was Spurgeon's "Robinson Crusoe's Text": in Defoe's book, Crusoe, near death on the island, opened a Bible to this verse and prayed for the first time in his life. — Enduring Word (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-50/); Spurgeon (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tod/psalms-50.html)

- "God prefers the prayer of a broken heart to the finest service that ever was performed by priests and choirs." — Spurgeon, cited in Enduring Word (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-50/)

## Verses 16–21: Rebuke of Hypocritical Wickedness

**v. 16: "To the wicked, however, God says, 'What right have you to recite My statutes and to bear My covenant on your lips?'"**

- The "wicked" here are still *within* the covenant community — they recite God's statutes and take His covenant in their mouth. They are not pagans but hypocritical professors. — Enduring Word (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-50/); Ellicott (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/50.htm); Constable (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/psalms-50.html)

- Gill identifies them as the Scribes, Pharisees and doctors among the Jews — teachers of the law whose lives contradicted their teaching. — Gill (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/50.htm)

- Pulpit Commentary: "They claim the privileges of God's covenanted servants, but perform none of the duties." — (search snippet)

- A poignant historical note: Origen, after his moral fall, opened the Bible to this very verse and was unable to preach, breaking into tears. — Enduring Word (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-50/), citing Trapp.

**v. 17: "For you hate My instruction and cast My words behind you."**

- This moves from inward alienation ("hate instruction") to open rejection ("cast My words behind you") — a progression of rebellion. — Pulpit Commentary (search snippet)

**v. 18: "When you see a thief, you befriend him, and throw in your lot with adulterers."**

- The charges represent the whole Decalogue: theft breaches the eighth commandment; adultery the seventh; deceit the ninth. — Enduring Word (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-50/), citing VanGemeren.

- Even consenting with sinners — befriending the thief, partnering with adulterers — brings one under the same condemnation. — Enduring Word (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-50/)

**v. 19: "You unleash your mouth for evil and unharness your tongue for deceit."**

- The Hebrew for "unleash" (*shalach*) means to let loose, and "harness" (or "frame") is literally "weave" — the tongue weaves deceit like a spider spins a web. — Ellicott (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/50.htm)

**v. 20: "You sit and malign your brother; you slander your own mother's son."**

- "Sit" (or "lurk") suggests sitting in ambush to speak against someone. — Ellicott (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/50.htm)

- "Mother's son" in a polygamous culture marks an even closer relationship than the more general "brother" — making the slander more heinous. — Ellicott (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/50.htm)

**v. 21: "You have done these things, and I kept silent; you thought I was just like you. But now I rebuke you and accuse you to your face."**

- This is the heart of the psalm: God's silence (His patience and longsuffering) was misinterpreted as indifference or approval. They forgot God's holiness and made Him in their own image — "you thought I was altogether like you." — Enduring Word (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-50/); Spurgeon (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tod/psalms-50.html); Constable (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/psalms-50.html)

- "God's silence is an emphatic way of expressing His patient tolerance of evil unpunished. Such longsuffering is meant to lead to repentance…but as experience shows, it is often abused." — Maclaren, cited in Enduring Word (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-50/)

- "Accuse you to your face" (or "set them in order before your eyes"): all the sins are marshalled before the sinner like an army in battle array. — Ellicott (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/50.htm)

## Verses 22–23: Conclusion — Warning and Promise

**v. 22: "Now consider this, you who forget God, lest I tear you to pieces, with no one to rescue you:"**

- "Consider this" (Hebrew *binah*): a call to take it to heart, to understand. "You who forget God" addresses both the ritualists (vv. 7–15) and the hypocrites (vv. 16–21), for both have "forgotten" God in different ways. — Enduring Word (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-50/); Cambridge Bible (search snippet: the epilogue sums up both groups)

- "Tear you to pieces" — the image is of a lion rending its prey, with none to deliver. — Spurgeon (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tod/psalms-50.html)

- Constable notes: "God let His people off with a warning." — Constable (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/psalms-50.html)

**v. 23: "He who sacrifices a thank offering honors Me, and to him who rights his way, I will show the salvation of God."**

- The two clauses correspond to the two charges: thank offering addresses the ritualism of vv. 7–15; "rights his way" addresses the hypocrisy of vv. 16–21. — Enduring Word (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-50/); Ellicott (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/50.htm)

- "Rights his way" (or "orders his conduct aright"): Ellicott suggests the Hebrew may imply "him who has *turned* his way" — i.e., repentance, a change of life. — Ellicott (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/50.htm)

- Crucially, neither thank offerings nor right living *earn* salvation. They simply put a person in the place to receive what God gives: "I will show the salvation of God." — Enduring Word (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-50/); Spurgeon: "He needs salvation, for the best ordering of the life cannot save us, but that salvation he shall have." — Spurgeon (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tod/psalms-50.html)

## Denominational Distinctives (What Could Be Found)

Given search/fetch limits, I was unable to retrieve dedicated teachings from denominational sites (Ligonier for Reformed, Desiring God / GTY for Baptist, Seedbed for Methodist/Wesleyan, 1517.org for Lutheran, AG.org for Pentecostal, OCA.org for Orthodox, Catholic.com, etc.). However, the commentaries I accessed come from various traditions:

- **Reformed / Baptist (Spurgeon, Gill, Constable, Enduring Word):** The consistent emphasis is that the psalm teaches the insufficiency of mere outward religion without a transformed heart. Spurgeon reads it Christologically — the "covenant by sacrifice" points to Christ's propitiatory sacrifice; the "saints" are the elect. Enduring Word (David Guzik, broadly evangelical/charismatic) applies it pastorally to believers under the New Covenant facing the "judgment seat of Christ" (2 Cor 5:10) — not for salvation but for reward. — Spurgeon (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tod/psalms-50.html); Enduring Word (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-50/)

- **Gill (Particular Baptist):** Reads the whole psalm as prophecy of the Gospel age — the calling of Gentiles, abrogation of ceremonial law, and judgment on the unbelieving Jews. He identifies the "wicked" as the Jewish religious leaders who rejected Christ. — Gill (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/50.htm)

- **Anglican (Ellicott):** Emphasizes the psalm's place within the prophetic tradition — the inseparable union of morality with religion. Ellicott was a Church of England bishop; his notes highlight the literary quality and the prophetic-ethical thrust. — Ellicott (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/50.htm)

- **Methodist/Holiness (Whedon, Clarke, Trapp — cited by others):** Trapp (Anglican Puritan) and Clarke (Methodist) are quoted throughout the sources. Clarke stresses that the people had begun to *trust* in their sacrifices rather than in God. Trapp calls out "carnal gospellers" who think they have served God merely by attending church. — Enduring Word (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-50/) citing Clarke and Trapp; Whedon (search snippet: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/whe/psalms-50.html)

## Summary of Key Traditional Teaching Themes

1. **God is the universal Judge** — the triple name (El, Elohim, Yahweh) underscores His absolute authority over all humanity.
2. **Judgment begins with God's own people** — this is the psalm's great "twist" and is echoed in 1 Peter 4:17.
3. **Ritual without relationship is worthless** — God does not need our sacrifices; He owns everything. What He wants is a thankful heart, obedient life, and trusting prayer.
4. **Hypocritical profession is a grave offense** — those who mouth God's words but live in disobedience mistake God's patience for approval and forget His holiness.
5. **The offer of grace remains open** — the psalm ends not in destruction but in invitation: genuine praise and a right-ordered life open the way to experience God's salvation.

*(Sources are cited under each verse above.)*
